title: Bad Santa
full_review:
You better watch out. You better not cry. You better not pout, I'm telling you why: A chain-smoking, skirt-chasing, foul-mouthed Santa is coming to town -- or at least to a theater near you.
Billy Bob Thornton stars in "Bad Santa" (Dimension), director Terry Zwigoff's bilious black comedy about a burned-out burglar who steals the "merry" out of Christmas.

Thornton plays Willie T. Stokes, a self-loathing, perpetually pickled safecracker who dons the red suit each holiday season and poses as a department store Santa in order to gain after-hours access to the store's loot.

Viewers first meet the lecherous lout sitting alone in a bar wearing a stained Santa outfit wallowing in misanthropic misery. After an astringent, Chopin-scored voice-over, a well-lubricated Willie stumbles out into the back alley and vomits just as the title card appears. Nothing puts an audience in the holiday spirit quite like a Currier & Ives upchucking.

The film then flashes forward a year. Willie is roused from his annual 11-month stupor when Marcus (Tony Cox), his dwarf accomplice -- the brains of the operation -- summons him to Phoenix where he has staked out a shopping mall ripe for the taking.

Right off the bat, Willie's rancid attitude and potty-mouthed rants raise red flags with the store's strait-laced manager (John Ritter, in his final role), who alerts the mall's chief of security (Bernie Mac) to the new hangdog hires.

After coming home to find the square-shield sniffing around his motel room, Willie hides out in the tony digs of Thurman (Brett Kelly), a friendless overweight 8-year-old whose white-collar criminal father is serving jail time, leaving the sad-sack kid alone in the house with only his senile grandmother (Cloris Leachman).

The two misfits strike up a co-dependent relationship, the youngster proving a most unlikely antidote to the yegg-nog's poisoned soul. After beating up a bunch of skate-boarding neighborhood bullies who had been terrorizing Thurman, Willie begins to feel the first stirrings of his booze-soaked conscience.

Willie also finds love -- or at least lust -- with a libidinous barmaid (Lauren Graham), who has a fetish for men in Santa suits. Being raised Jewish, she never got a chance to sit on Santa's lap and is now apparently making up for lost time.

In fairness, it is somewhat of a misnomer that the film presents Santa in a sleazy light, since Thornton's character is not Kris Kringle but only a store stand-in. Still, Zwigoff deserves coal in his stocking for soiling Santa's red suit (in more ways than one) by dragging a beloved symbol of Christmas into the proverbial gutter -- and barely avoiding an NC-17 rating in the process.

Given the crass commercialization of Christmas which has systematically stripped it of its religious significance, it should not be surprising that such a caustic bashing of one of the holiday's most beloved symbols isn't met with public indignation.

Far from raising eyebrows, the film has earned praise from many critics as a welcome relief to the sugarplum sentimentality of more traditional yuletide yarns. Such positive reviews seem to underline the toxic bah-humbug cynicism that has infected modern secular society.

In addition to assaulting viewers with a nonstop barrage of obscenities, the film's "naughty" list includes several raunchy sexual encounters (though nudity is surprisingly absent) and repeated use of the "f word" in scenes involving young children. Much of the film's ribald one-note humor is fueled by the prevailing belief that if it is offensive it's funny, and if it is heartless it's hip. Though perfectly cast as the soused scrooge, Thornton scowls through the film sounding like a foul-mouthed Grinch.

And while the twisted tale does offer a whisper of repentance and redemption, the film's criticism of consumer culture is a clear case of too little, too late and is hardly commensurate with the steady stream of smut leading up to it.

Rather than applauding Zwigoff for such a determinedly mean-spirited attack on Christmas, perhaps he deserves, in the words of Charles Dickens, to be "boiled with his own pudding and buried with a stake of holly in his heart."

Due to excessive rough and crude language and profanity, recurring lewd sexual encounters, much crass humor, pervasive alcohol abuse, an attempted suicide and some violence, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
